newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa better after night of chest pains.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa better after night of chest pains.

text.p: Mother Teresa was feeling better on Monday following an uneasy night of chest pain and lung congestion, a doctor treating the revered nun said.
"Mother Teresa had chest pain last night and a lung congestion problem," said a doctor at Calcutta's Woodlands nursing home, where she is being treated. "She is better now."

The doctor, who asked not to be identified, said the medical board treating the 86-year-old Roman Catholic nun would wait until Wednesday to decide whether to carry out an angioplasty procedure, which involves inserting a balloon into a clogged arterial passage and then inflating it.
Mother Teresa earlier on Sunday had suffered heart failure for the third time in four days.

Known as the "Saint of the Gutters" for her work with the world's downtrodden, Mother Teresa suffered left ventricular heart failure late on Thursday night and was admitted to hospital early on Friday. It was the third time since August she had been admitted for emergency care.
She had begun recovering on Saturday and told doctors she wanted to go home.
But Dr Dinamani Banerjee, a member of the panel treating the Nobel Peace Prize winner, said she suffered left ventricular heart failure on Saturday night and again on Sunday morning.
"She is more stable than she was on Thursday night but recurrence of heart failure needs more investigation and we are not releasing her soon," Banerjee said.

The doctor said Mother Teresa was being given oxygen from time to time and her problem was being treated with medication. She was in the intensive-care cardiac unit but not in critical condition. Sister Mitra, a nurse in charge of the cardiac unit at Woodlands Nursing Home, said Mother Teresa had spoken to nuns from her Missionaries of Charity religious order and had written a letter before the weekend relapse of heart problems.
Fitted with a pacemaker in 1989, Mother Teresa has since spent time in hospital for heart disease, bacterial pneumonia, broken ribs, malaria, and lung problems.
She spent nearly three weeks at Woodlands in August and September for heart trouble, malaria and pneumonia.
Two weeks after returning to her Calcutta-based order, she fell off a chair and hit her head. A brain scan revealed a blood clot in the brain. She was released after it disappeared.
Last Saturday, Mother Teresa received honorary American citizenship, one of only five people to do so in U.S. history, in a ceremony led by U.S. Ambassador to India Frank Wisner.
She began her life's work helping the poor in the slums of Calcutta, India's most densely populated city, in 1949.
